arXiv:2403.17602v1 [math.CO] 26 Mar 2024

A method of constructing pairwise balanced designs containing parallel classes

Douglas R. Stinson ††thanks: D.R. Stinson’s research is supported by NSERC discovery grant RGPIN-03882. Affiliation: David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Waterloo Affiliation: Waterloo ON, N2L 3G1, Canada
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The obvious way to construct a GDD (group-divisible design) recursively is to use Wilson’s Fundamental Construction for GDDs (WFC). Then a PBD (pairwise balanced design) is often obtained by adding a new point to each group of the GDD. However, after constructing such a PBD, it might be the case that we then want to identify a parallel class of blocks. In this short note, we explore some possible ways of doing this.

1 Introduction and Definitions

We use standard design-theoretic terminology for GDDs (group-divisible designs), PBDs (pairwise balanced designs) and transversal designs (TDs). To begin, we recall a few definitions of these kinds of designs from [1].

Let KK and LL be sets of positive integers (we can assume that every element of KK is at least two). A KK-group-divisible design (or KK-GDD) with group sizes in LL is a triple (X,𝒢,𝒜)(X,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{A}) that satisfies the following properties:

  1. 1.

    XX is a set of points.

  2. 2.

    𝒢\mathcal{G} is a partition of XX into groups such that |G|∈L|G|\in L for all G∈𝒢G\in\mathcal{G}.

  3. 3.

    𝒜\mathcal{A} consists of a set of blocks such that

    1. (a)

      |G∩A|≤1|G\cap A|\leq 1 for all G∈𝒢G\in\mathcal{G} and for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A},

    2. (b)

      every pair of points from different groups is contained in exactly one block, and

    3. (c)

      |A|∈K|A|\in K for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}.

If K={k}K=\{k\}, we write kk-GDD for simplicity. The type of the GDD is the multiset {|G|:G∈𝒢}\{|G|:G\in\mathcal{G}\}. We usually employ an exponential notation to describe types: type t1u1​t2u2​…{t_{1}}^{u_{1}}{t_{2}}^{u_{2}}\dots denotes uiu_{i} occurrences of tit_{i} for i=1,2,…i=1,2,\dots.

A TD(k,m)(k,m) (or transversal design)is a kk-GDD of type mkm^{k}. Thus every block in a transversal design is a transversal of the kk groups. It is well-known that a TD(k,m)(k,m) is equivalent to k−2k-2 mutually orthogonal latin squares of order mm.

Let KK be a set of positive integers. A (v,K)(v,K)-pairwise balanced design (or (v,K)(v,K)-PBD) is a pair (X,𝒜)(X,\mathcal{A}) that satisfies the following properties:

  1. 1.

    XX is a set of points,

  2. 2.

    𝒜\mathcal{A} consists of a set of blocks such that every pair of points is contained in exactly one block, and

  3. 3.

    |A|∈K|A|\in K for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}.

If K={k}K=\{k\}, we write (v,k)(v,k)-PBD for simplicity. A (v,k)(v,k)-PBD is also known as a (v,k,1)(v,k,1)-balanced incomplete block design (or (v,k,1)(v,k,1)-BIBD).

If qq is a prime or prime power, then there exists a (q2,q,1)(q^{2},q,1)-BIBD (an affine plane of order qq) and a (q2+q+1,q+1,1)(q^{2}+q+1,q+1,1)-BIBD (a projective plane of order qq).

Before describing our constructions for PBDs containing parallel classes, we recall Wilson’s Fundamental Construction for GDDs (which we abbreviate to WFC). We follow the presentation from [1, §IV.2.1].

Construction 1.1 (Wilson’s Fundamental Construction for GDDs).

Suppose that (X,𝒢,𝒜)(X,\mathcal{G},\mathcal{A}) is a GDD and let w:X→ℤ+w:X\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{+} (ww is called a weighting). For every block A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}, suppose there is a KK-GDD of type {w⁡(x):x∈A}\{w(x):x\in A\}. For all G∈𝒢G\in\mathcal{G}, define wG=∑x∈Gw⁡(x)w_{G}=\sum_{x\in G}w(x). Then there is a KK-GDD of type {wG:G∈𝒢}\{w_{G}:G\in\mathcal{G}\}.

2 Constructions

We often construct GDDs recursively using Construction 1.1. Then a PBD can be obtained from the resulting GDD by adding a new point to each group. Suppose, after constructing such a PBD, that we then want to identify a parallel class of blocks. Our next theorem provides one way to accomplish this goal.

Theorem 2.1.

Suppose there is a TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m) and a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u), where u≤mu\leq m. Suppose ℓ∈K\ell\in K and suppose that there is a KK-GDD of type uℓ​v1u^{\ell}v^{1}. Finally, suppose there exists an (m​u+1,K)(mu+1,K)-PBD. Then there exists a KK-GDD of type ℓm​u​(t​v+1)1\ell^{mu}{(tv+1)}^{1} for all tt such that 0≤t≤m−u0\leq t\leq m-u.

Proof.

Start with a TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m) and delete m−tm-t points from the last group. This yields an ({ℓ,ℓ+1},1)(\{\ell,\ell+1\},1)-GDD of type mℓ​t1m^{\ell}t^{1}. The blocks have sizes ℓ\ell and ℓ+1\ell+1 and every block of size ℓ+1\ell+1 intersects the last group. Give every point in the first ℓ\ell groups weight uu, give every point in the last group weight vv, and apply Construction 1.1 (WFC). For a block of size ℓ\ell, we fill in a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u). For a block of size ℓ+1\ell+1, we fill in a KK-GDD of type uℓ​v1u^{\ell}v^{1}.

We now have a KK-GDD of type (m​u)ℓ​(t​v)1(mu)^{\ell}(tv)^{1}. Let ∞\infty be a new point. Replace every group GG of size m​umu by an (m​u+1,K)(mu+1,K)-PBD on G∪{∞}G\cup\{\infty\}. Also, add ∞\infty to the last group. This produces an (m​u​ℓ+t​v+1,K∪{t​v+1})(mu\ell+tv+1,K\cup\{tv+1\})-PBD.

It remains to identify a parallel class of blocks in this PBD. The parallel class will consist of m​umu blocks of size ℓ\ell and the block of size t​v+1tv+1. Choose uu of the points that were deleted from the last group of the TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m) (note that u≤m−tu\leq m-t). These uu points induce uu classes of mm blocks of size ℓ\ell, each of which partitions the points in the first ℓ\ell groups of the TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m). Denote these classes by 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, 1≤i≤u1\leq i\leq u.

When we apply WFC, we replace every point xx by a set of uu points, say {x}×{1,…,u}\{x\}\times\{1,\dots,u\}. Every block BB of size ℓ\ell is replaced by the u2u^{2} blocks in a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u), in which the groups are {x}×{1,…,u}\{x\}\times\{1,\dots,u\}, x∈Bx\in B. For all B∈𝒫iB\in\mathcal{P}_{i} (where 1≤i≤u1\leq i\leq u), we can stipulate that B′={(x,i):x∈B}B^{\prime}=\{(x,i):x\in B\} is one of the blocks in the TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) constructed from BB.

Now define

𝒫={B′:B∈𝒫i,1≤i≤u}.\mathcal{P}=\{B^{\prime}:B\in\mathcal{P}_{i},1\leq i\leq u\}.

It is easily seen that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a set of m​umu blocks of size ℓ\ell that form a partition of the first ℓ\ell groups of the KK-GDD of type (m​u)ℓ​(t​v)1(mu)^{\ell}(tv)^{1}. In the constructed PBD, there is a unique block B0B_{0} of size t​v+1tv+1 arising from the last group of the TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m) together with ∞\infty. The blocks in 𝒫\mathcal{P}, along with B0B_{0}, comprise the desired parallel class. This parallel class is taken to be the groups in a KK-GDD of type ℓm​u​(t​v+1)1\ell^{mu}{(tv+1)}^{1}. ∎

Here is a specific application of Theorem 2.1.

Corollary 2.2.

Suppose m≡0m\equiv 0 or 1mod51\bmod 5, m>10m>10, and let 0≤t≤m−40\leq t\leq m-4. Then there exists a 55-GDD of type 54​m​(4​t+1)15^{4m}{(4t+1)}^{1}.

Proof.

We apply Theorem 2.1 with ℓ=5\ell=5, u=v=4u=v=4 and K={5}K=\{5\}. A KK-GDD of type uℓ​v1u^{\ell}v^{1} is just a 55-GDD of type 464^{6}, which is obtained from an affine plane of order 55 with a point deleted. A TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) is obtained from a projective plane of order 44 by deleting a point. A TD(6,m)(6,m) exists from [1, §III.3.6]. An (m​u+1,K)(mu+1,K)-PBD is just a (4​m+1,5,1)(4m+1,5,1)-BIBD, which exists because m≡0m\equiv 0 or 1mod51\bmod 5 (see [1, §II.3.1]). We obtain a 55-GDD of type 54​m​(4​t+1)15^{4m}{(4t+1)}^{1}. ∎

Remark.

The constructed PBD has blocks of size five and a block of size 4​t+14t+1. Many results on such PBDs are known, e.g., see [1, §IV.1.2]. But there is apparently less information known on when such a PBD contains a parallel class that includes the block of size 4​t+14t+1.

Here is one small numerical example to illustrate.

Example 2.3.

We construct 55-GDDs of type 544​s15^{44}s^{1} for s=1,5,…,29s=1,5,\dots,29. Take m=11m=11, let t=0,1,…,7t=0,1,\dots,7 and apply Corollary 2.2.

We next observe that we can improve Theorem 2.1 if we have some information about the existence of disjoint blocks in the TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u).

Theorem 2.4.

Suppose there is a TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m). Suppose also that there is a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) containing α\alpha disjoint blocks, where u≤mu\leq m. Suppose ℓ∈K\ell\in K and suppose that there is a KK-GDD of type uℓ​v1u^{\ell}v^{1}. Finally, suppose there exists an (m​u+1,K)(mu+1,K)-PBD. Then there exists a KK-GDD of type ℓm​u​(t​v+1)1\ell^{mu}{(tv+1)}^{1} for all tt such that 0≤t≤m−⌈u/α⌉0\leq t\leq m-\lceil u/\alpha\rceil.

Proof.

The construction of the (muℓ+tv+1,{K,(tv+1)∗)(mu\ell+tv+1,\{K,(tv+1)^{*})-PBD is the same as in the proof of Theorem 2.1. However, we construct the parallel class of blocks of size ℓ\ell slightly differently. Choose ⌈u/α⌉\lceil u/\alpha\rceil of the points that were deleted from the last group of the TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m) (note that ⌈u/α⌉≤m−t\lceil u/\alpha\rceil\leq m-t). These ⌈u/α⌉\lceil u/\alpha\rceil points induce ⌈u/α⌉\lceil u/\alpha\rceil classes of mm blocks of size ℓ\ell, each of which partitions the points in the first ℓ\ell groups of the TD(ℓ+1,m)(\ell+1,m). Denote these classes by 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, 1≤i≤⌈u/α⌉1\leq i\leq\lceil u/\alpha\rceil.

When we apply WFC, we replace every point xx by a set of uu points, say {x}×{1,…,u}\{x\}\times\{1,\dots,u\}. Every block B∈𝒫iB\in\mathcal{P}_{i} is replaced by the u2u^{2} blocks in a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) in which the groups are {x}×{1,…,u}\{x\}\times\{1,\dots,u\}, x∈Bx\in B.

Partition the set {1,…,u}\{1,\dots,u\} into ⌈u/α⌉\lceil u/\alpha\rceil disjoint sets, say T1,…,T⌈u/α⌉T_{1},\dots,T_{\lceil u/\alpha\rceil}, each of size at most α\alpha. Each TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) contains α\alpha disjoint blocks. For 1≤i≤⌈u/α⌉1\leq i\leq\lceil u/\alpha\rceil, for each B∈𝒫iB\in\mathcal{P}_{i} and every j∈Tij\in T_{i}, define Bj′={(x,j):x∈B}B^{\prime}_{j}=\{(x,j):x\in B\}. We can stipulate that the α\alpha blocks Bj′B^{\prime}_{j} (for all j∈Tij\in T_{i}) are blocks in the TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) constructed from BB.

Now define

𝒫={Bj′:B∈𝒫i,1≤i≤⌈u/α⌉,j∈Ti}.\mathcal{P}=\{B^{\prime}_{j}:B\in\mathcal{P}_{i},1\leq i\leq\lceil u/\alpha\rceil,j\in T_{i}\}.

It is easily seen that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a set of m​umu blocks of size ℓ\ell that form a partition of the first ℓ\ell groups of the KK-GDD of type (m​u)ℓ​(t​v)1(mu)^{\ell}(tv)^{1}. The rest of the construction proceeds as before. ∎

Remark.

The advantage of Theorem 2.4 (with α>1\alpha>1) as compared to Theorem 2.1 is that we can take larger values of tt in Theorem 2.4.

In order to apply Theorem 2.4, we need to know something about disjoint blocks in a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u). This problem has been studied extensively in the case ℓ=3\ell=3, where a set of disjoint blocks is a partial transversal of the associated latin square. See Wanless [3] for a survey of results on this problem. We briefly mention a few general results for arbitrary ℓ\ell that are well-known and/or follow from elementary counting arguments.

Lemma 2.5.

 


  1. 1.

    If there is a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u), then ℓ≤u+1\ell\leq u+1.

  2. 2.

    A TD(u+1,u)(u+1,u) does not contain two disjoint blocks.

  3. 3.

    A TD(u,u)(u,u) contains uu disjoint blocks.

  4. 4.

    If there is a TD(ℓ+1,u)(\ell+1,u), then there is a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) that contains uu disjoint blocks.

  5. 5.

    A TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) with u≥ℓ≥2u\geq\ell\geq 2 contains at least three disjoint blocks, unless u=ℓ=2u=\ell=2.

  6. 6.

    A TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) contains at least ⌈u2ℓ⁡(u−1)+1⌉\left\lceil\frac{u^{2}}{\ell(u-1)+1}\right\rceil disjoint blocks.

Proof.

Parts 1.–4. are well-known, so we only provide a proof of parts 5 and 6. First we prove part 5. A block BB in a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) intersects ℓ⁡(u−1)\ell(u-1) other blocks. There are u2u^{2} blocks. Hence, there exists a block disjoint from BB if and only if u2>1+ℓ⁡(u−1)u^{2}>1+\ell(u-1), or ℓ<u+1\ell<u+1. Since ℓ≤u\ell\leq u, there are at least two disjoint blocks. Now, assume that B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} are disjoint blocks. There are ℓ⁡(ℓ−1)\ell(\ell-1) blocks that intersect both B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}. Since every point is in uu blocks, there are 2​ℓ​(u−ℓ)2\ell(u-\ell) blocks that contain exactly one point from B1∪B2B_{1}\cup B_{2}. It follows that there is a block disjoint from both B1B_{1} and B2B_{2} if and only if u2−2​ℓ​(u−ℓ)−ℓ⁡(ℓ−1)−2>0u^{2}-2\ell(u-\ell)-\ell(\ell-1)-2>0. Fix ℓ\ell and define

f⁡(u)=u2−2​ℓ​(u−ℓ)−ℓ⁡(ℓ−1)−2.f(u)=u^{2}-2\ell(u-\ell)-\ell(\ell-1)-2.

We have f′​(u)=2​(u−ℓ)≥0f^{\prime}(u)=2(u-\ell)\geq 0 if u≥ℓu\geq\ell. Also, f⁡(ℓ)=ℓ−2>0f(\ell)=\ell-2>0 since ℓ>2\ell>2. It follows that f⁡(u)>0f(u)>0 for all u≥ℓu\geq\ell when ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3. When ℓ=2\ell=2, we have f⁡(u)=(u−2)2f(u)=(u-2)^{2}, so f⁡(u)>0f(u)>0 if and only if u>2u>2. This establishes the existence of three disjoint blocks in the TD, unless u=ℓ=2u=\ell=2.

To prove part 6, let B1,…,BrB_{1},\dots,B_{r} be a maximal set of rr disjoint blocks in a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u). Denote Y=⋃i=1rBiY=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}B_{i}. Since we started with a maximal set of disjoint blocks, there is no block disjoint from YY. Denote the set of u2−ru^{2}-r blocks other than B1,…,BrB_{1},\dots,B_{r} by ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime}. For B∈ℬ′B\in\mathcal{B}^{\prime}, define aB=|B∩Y|a_{B}=|B\cap Y|. By assumption, aB≥1a_{B}\geq 1 for all B∈ℬ′B\in\mathcal{B}^{\prime}. We have

∑B∈ℬ′aB=r​ℓ​(u−1).\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}^{\prime}}a_{B}=r\ell(u-1).

Therefore the mean of the aBa_{B}’s is

a¯=r​ℓ​(u−1)u2−r.\overline{a}=\frac{r\ell(u-1)}{u^{2}-r}.

Since a¯≥1\overline{a}\geq 1, we have

r​ℓ​(u−1)u2−r≥1,\frac{r\ell(u-1)}{u^{2}-r}\geq 1,

or

r​ℓ​(u−1)≥u2−r.r\ell(u-1)\geq u^{2}-r.

Consequently,

r≥u2ℓ⁡(u−1)+1.r\geq\frac{u^{2}}{\ell(u-1)+1}.

Hence, the TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) contains at least ⌈u2ℓ⁡(u−1)+1⌉\left\lceil\frac{u^{2}}{\ell(u-1)+1}\right\rceil disjoint blocks. ∎

Remarks.
  1. 1.

    Wilson’s 1974 construction for mutually orthogonal latin squares [4] explicitly makes use of transversal designs containing disjoint blocks. Also, it is observed in [4] that a TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) contains at least two disjoint blocks if ℓ≤u\ell\leq u.

  2. 2.

    We observe that Corollary 2.2 is a special case of Theorem 2.4 in which α=1\alpha=1. In view of Lemma 2.5, we cannot take α>1\alpha>1 in this case because ℓ=u+1\ell=u+1.

  3. 3.

    The bound proven in part 6 also follows from a more general result due to Rosenfeld [2, Theorem I b)].

Here is an example of an application of Theorem 2.4 with α=u\alpha=u.

Corollary 2.6.

Suppose exists a TD(8,m)(8,m) and a (7​m+1,7,1)(7m+1,7,1)-BIBD and let 0≤t≤m−10\leq t\leq m-1. Then there exists a {7,8}\{7,8\}-GDD of type 77​m​(7​t+1)17^{7m}{(7t+1)}^{1}.

Proof.

We apply Theorem 2.4 with ℓ=u=v=α=7\ell=u=v=\alpha=7 and K={7,8}K=\{7,8\}. A projective plane of order 77 with a point deleted yields an 88-GDD of type 787^{8}, which is a KK-GDD of type uℓ​v1u^{\ell}v^{1}. A TD(ℓ,u)(\ell,u) with α\alpha disjoint blocks is obtained from a affine plane of order 77 (one parallel class yields the groups and a second parallel class yields α\alpha disjoint blocks). A (7​m+1,7,1)(7m+1,7,1)-BIBD, which exists by hypothesis, is an (m​u+1,K)(mu+1,K)-PBD. We obtain a {7,8}\{7,8\}-GDD of type 77​m​(7​t+1)17^{7m}{(7t+1)}^{1}. ∎

Remark.

It is known (see [1, §II.3.1]) that (7​m+1,7,1)(7m+1,7,1)-BIBDs exist for m≡0​ or ​1mod6m\equiv 0\text{ or }1\bmod 6, m>372m>372. Also, T​D​(8,m)TD(8,m) are known to exist for all m>74m>74. So Corollary 2.6 can be applied for all m≡0​ or ​1mod6m\equiv 0\text{ or }1\bmod 6, m>372m>372.
